account: Pirotta and colleagues tested AI detection of marine wildlife in three-dimensional X-ray scans. Their June 8, 2026 paper reports 298 scans from 68 specimens, including preserved specimens and fresh shark material. The researchers expanded the scans by inserting specimen images into baggage images. A 512-bag test set contained both original scans and these synthetic composites, drawn from the same specimen population. Table 3 reports detection rates of 95% for shark fins, 96% for seahorses, and 86% for sea cucumbers. The overall false-alarm rate was 13%; the class-specific rates were 2%, 9%, and 1%. Rapiscan supplied equipment and funded staff participation in analysis and writing. The paper demonstrates laboratory detection, with no reported operational seizure or customs evaluation.

ai_role.statement: AI classified objects in CT baggage scans. Most positive test bags used synthetically inserted specimens, and testing drew from the same specimen population. The paper is original research with disclosed Rapiscan involvement, not an independent deployment evaluation.

claim_basis: Sources: the makers' peer-reviewed study. The cited evidence includes no independent source and no finding by a regulator or court.

fields.account: Pirotta and colleagues tested AI detection of marine wildlife in three-dimensional X-ray scans. Their June 8, 2026 paper reports 298 scans from 68 specimens, including preserved specimens and fresh shark material. The researchers expanded the scans by inserting specimen images into baggage images. A 512-bag test set contained both original scans and these synthetic composites, drawn from the same specimen population. Table 3 reports detection rates of 95% for shark fins, 96% for seahorses, and 86% for sea cucumbers. The overall false-alarm rate was 13%; the class-specific rates were 2%, 9%, and 1%. Rapiscan supplied equipment and funded staff participation in analysis and writing. The paper demonstrates laboratory detection, with no reported operational seizure or customs evaluation.
